title: Show HN: Crosswalk – terminal manager to reduce sprawl
text:
I usually have many projects and terminals I’m working in so Crosswalk groups my work together and allows me to open a terminal (or another terminal app) in the correct folder/project quickly and label the tab (as well as add notes). I started on iTerm2 (which is great) years ago for my terminal manager, then found I spent too much time flipping between tabs once I started leveraging terminal agents like Claude Code and Codex so I built Crosswalk to improve visibility at a glance. It originally started as a web page, but then I moved it to an app so I had better control over notifications and sounds to let me know when work was done or needed me on one of the tabs.

Crosswalk shows which sessions are still working or sitting idle with an activity dot on the tab. It provides hotkeys to jump between tabs and groups quickly. Even if you're not using agents, you can still use it for your terminal work - I commonly leave active projects as groups on the left even if I not working in them right now. There's an MCP server so an agent can launch new tabs (and agents) - it's helpful when you need a lead agent to spawn long running agents (in visible tabs) and then monitor their status (running, stuck, needs user feedback) or compact their context at efficient times. There are other nice features like layouts to view multiple terminals at once and reopens terminals from last session. I spent a bunch of time iterating on the pty host (pseudoterminal host) so updating the app or closing and then reopening will restore the sessions.

This is a paid product you can trial for free. I created it to solve the multi agent bottlenecks so I use it daily, both personally and professionally. For Mac and Windows - Electron based.
author: josephspurrier

title: Ask HN: What mistakes did AI make in your codebase?
text:
In the past few weeks I've beeing working with frontier AI - Opus 5.5, Astra, Sol 6.1, Fable 5.1 and Gemini Argon.

AI has become really good at coding in some sense, that's undeniable, and there are people that say you don't really need to review their code anymore.

But I keep getting stuck in a sensation that's between cognitive dissonance, FOMO, and a vague sense of being gaslit, because when I review the code it writes - and this is all of them - 80% of it is right, and 20% is wrong, but in extremely subtle ways; only when you deeply understand the system and carefully review it do you spot the issues. These are not stylistic choices, the code is incorrect. Of course, the AI fixes it when you prompt it to, but you need to work very hard to know what needs prompting.

This is all after the grill-me skills and cross-model adversarial review and whatnot (all these techniques do help somewhat but they didn't get it perfect),

For example, I had AI (Opus 5.5 and Gemini both tried, in this particular case) write an integration test for our system, to reproduce an issue we had. It failed because it chose, for simplicity, to combine two backend fakes into one store, having writes covered by the same mutex, but the bug was only happening in production when these two stores went out of sync (and they did because we wrote to both concurrently and one write failed). (I don't want to argue the merits of the design. This is existing code.)

The wrong code it wrote to try and find the issue was carefully written, well organized, function names were reasonable, etc. etc.

I can't be alone in this, but I can't put my finger on what exactly goes wrong in the process.

Can you share examples of changes you wanted to make that Claude and the bunch (frontier versions) got subtly wrong?

title: Re: "AI for everyone would cost a tenth of a kettle a ...
text:
Wouldn't it be really nice if these values were required to be published, with strong legal oversight, and meaningful financial penalties should there be mistakes?

Why should I need to trust a corporate white paper/preprint from an AI company? Why should I need to trust a CEO from an AI company? What fine points are omitted?

But, let's do it this way. How does something with the energy demand of only a tenth of a kettle per day per person put such a strain on the UK's grid - a country which boils many kettles every day - that there's a demand to increase power generation by 50%?

Ofgem reported earlier this year, at https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2026-02/2026-02... :

"NESO received a total of 229 responses to its CFI. The CFI identified around 140 (50 GW) data centres, the majority of which are likely to receive a Gate 2 offer. 71 (around 20 GW) data centres reported they have achieved financial commitment with FID."

and

"Since November 2024, total contracted offers in the demand queue rose sharply from 41 GW (17 GW Transmission, 24 GW Distribution) to 125 GW (97 GW Transmission, 29 GW Distribution) in June 2025. For comparison, peak electricity demand in GB on 11 February 2026 was 45 GW."

It's almost as if scaling up the median Gemini text prompt use from last year's preprint has very little bearing on the total AI power use.

After all, we know there are far more AI uses than the two presented options of "thirty Gemini queries per day" and "every adult makes one AI video a day".

title: Re: It wasn't AI that flipped Proton's charge...
text:
I'm a paying proton customer, I migrated last year from the horror that is Office365 (or Copilot 365 or whatever they call it now) and before that I migrated from Google Workspace. In direct comparisson, proton is the best product for me - and that does not include privacy or security things, just stuff like generall UX and featureset. Yes, they have some annoying bugs, but so did the others.

I think the AI backlash against Proton so far is unwarranted. It is purely speculative and based on make-belief. I am a dev myself, I use AI more and more, and I have no more long-term experience than the next dev. But so far the claim that using AI in your corp and workflow will result in buggier, shitty code is not true on a broad scale. It is certainly not true for proton, at least I don't see service quality detiorating for my service. I think it is a tool, and what you get out of using it still depends on the skill of the craftsman.

As a customer, I do demand stable service and the promised saftey and security. But I also demand low prices and a product that can compete with the market. Now, the market is Google and Microsoft - two companies we don't even need to question if they lay off people due to AI usage. Proton is kind of under pressure to compete on a product level in a pretty much david-against-goliath situation. We see AI-assisted exploits such as the Linux use-after-free from Anthropic and can't blame Proton for restructuring their dev process to incorporate AI to find exactly these kind of security issues. I wouldn't even feel comfortable as a client if proton whipped on a "human code only" label on their services.

title: Re: Ask HN: What is a good open-weight alternative to ...
text:
Your terminology is a bit wrong. "Claude Code" has no "weights." It's a harness. It contacts Anthropic servers and runs their closed weight models.

The harness provides a means for the LLM to write file output and run tools (commands) to test output. Alternative harnesses including things like OpenCode.

You can point OpenCode to your Anthropic account, but only if you have API usage (there are ways around this, but if Anthropic detects it you could get banned). Anthropic locks their subscription plans to THEIR harness and no others.

Most harnesses like OpenCode, Cursor, Pi, Hermes, etc. have settings to tie into a bunch of different providers (although they'll always try to promote their own by default, because they have to fund their own harness development of course).

I recommend OpenCode + OpenRouter. OpenRouter has a bunch of models and their web interface shows where those models are run (AWS Bedrock, xAI, Anthropic, etc.) and what data they collect from your prompts (although this is kinda a 'trust me bro' status as a provider could be lying about collecting data).

title: Show HN: Breath of the Wild's Hyrule digital diorama
text:
Two weeks ago I posted a Zelda timeline here ahead of the Ocarina of Time remake. Here's what I've been working on: Breath of the Wild's Hyrule as a small 3D diorama you can explore. It has the main landmarks and a few easter eggs. It was the last Zelda game I played, early in the pandemic on a Wii U. It's been a fun little hit of nostalgia revisiting those places.

The terrain information comes from data the Zelda modding community which was then smoothed and scaled down. It's Three.js with the lighting and shadows baked when the page loads.

I built it with Claude, as I did the timeline. Without it, I'd never have had the time for a project this whimsical, so it wouldn't have seen the light of day. I didn't write any of the code. For me it felt a lot like part of being a tech lead: shaping the ideas and the output.

title: Show HN: Learn to beatmatch on Winamp-skinned decks (vibe-coded, desktop only)
text:
## Intro

Given all the token resets in the last few weeks, I decided to try building a fully vibe, and fully one-shotted project (one prompt per feature/bug fix, no reviews, neither human nor indipendent agents, only the ones the agent itself spawns).

That's how bit-cheer https://bit-cheer.com was born, a tool for learning beatmatching that I really wish I had when I started with turntables. The idea is absolutely not new, and if you want to learn beatmatching and want something much more tested and still free, I recommend https://www.beatmatch.pro/.

I needed a somewhat challenging task to see how far I could get with this 100% vibe, one-shotted approach, and I liked the somewhat nostalgic idea of using early 2000s graphics, so bit-cheer reuses Winamp's graphics and elements and can "wear" any Winamp skin.

## No mobile

The app was intentionally designed not to support mobile. I didn't feel like going crazy trying to make Winamp skins work on mobile, and it most likely never will support it.

## Technical details

The web app is written in Elm (with a bit of js, mainly for plumbing and skin rendering) and uses an audio engine written in Rust and compiled to WASM. That's all I know. (I had to ask the agent what it uses npm and js for, and it used for what I was more or less expecting)

What I didn't expect is that, for some reason, it decided not to use elm-test, so the score matcher, which according to the agent needs unit tests, is written entirely in JS. Two other unexpected things are (1) the Comfort/HD feature, which does pixel enhancement and is pretty CPU-heavy, is in js even though Rust/WASM was an option, and (2) the Vite and Elm dependencies are not up to date.

These are the only three issues that came out of a very quick review (literally a handful of questions to the agent). Everything else was done purely as a "user", meaning using the app and giving my feedback to the agent.

Most of the skin rendering was done by Claude with Opus 5.5 Max, while most of the audio engine was done by Astra 6 Ultra. The FE is 50/50.

I find that what I got is a very good result, considering that I give the agent only few high level instructions and then only used the app and reported bug and asked for features.

## The webapp

The webapp offers 5 modes:

* Foundation: you need to match 2 different kicks, and you can see the BPM of each track.

* Loop builder: you need to match 2 complete loops (many instruments, not just a kick), and you can see the BPM (you can build your own loops as well).

* By ear: same as loop builder, but BPMs are hidden.

* Star mode: same as by ear, but BPMs are not constant and you need to keep the tracks aligned.

* Pro decks: you can play actual music, 40 CC tracks or tracks you load from your PC. You can enable star mode here as well to keep things more interesting.

In any mode, you have a coach that will rate your run.

It also offer an 8 lesson learning path an hardwar mixed support (still not tested) and, of course, the skin studio.

title: Re: Japan's trains are great. Why is booking one so ha...
text:
I don't know for sure, but after living in Japan for 5 years now, whenever something in a Japanese business feels antiquated, inefficient, or just plain backwards and wrong, it's usually because some manager in an office who has been there longer than everyone else decided that it's good enough.

It probably sounds like I'm exaggerating, but loyalty to the hierarchy goes deep here. I don't know how many times I've had to hold my tongue and not state a fact because if I did, the manager would "lose face". Not an insult, a criticism, or even an open question, just a fact-- if I know it's contrary to what a manager thinks is the right way, he gets to sit back and keep his ego puffed up for no good reason.

Once my manager asked me to aggregate a list in excel to find a final count for a range of parts used in our blueprints. I used a pivot table in Excel. It took me about two minutes. He snapped back, "How are you doing this so quickly? It must be wrong. Do it like this:" and he proceeded to take a screenshot of each page of the sheet, send the screenshots to chatGPT, and ask it to aggregate them. Dear god I wish I was joking. It took him over an hour and still left room open for human error (or AI error I guess). I showed him the pivot table method, he just scoffed and walked away.
